one_liner: Single-header C99 Fortune-sweep 2D Voronoi/Delaunay generator, 1.4-3.7x faster than Boost.Polygon voronoi on random points.
what_it_does: jc_voronoi builds a clipped 2D Voronoi diagram (or Delaunay adjacency only) from a point set with one C call, jcv_diagram_generate(num_points, points, rect, clipper, &diagram), and frees it with jcv_diagram_free. It returns sites with counter-clockwise per-cell edge iterators, a global edge iterator, a Delaunay edge iterator and, since 0.10, packed unique-vertex indices. Edges are clipped to a box or, through jc_voronoi_clip.h, a convex polygon. It is not a drop-in for Boost.Polygon: point sites only (no segment sites), float by default (double via macros), and a C struct API instead of Boost's half-edge graph.
how_it_is_fast: It is Fortune's sweep-line algorithm with: an introsort specialized for jcv_site (y-then-x order; already-sorted input returns at once, reversed input is reversed in place); a binary-heap event queue specialized for half-edges; and, since 0.10, a rank-balanced relaxed AVL (RAVL) tree that indexes the beachline, replacing a linked scan that went quadratic on adversarial input (the 100k issue48 case fell from 9.15 s to 18.63 ms). Memory comes from a few large blocks (one up-front block for sites and events, then 16 KiB arenas), so a 100k diagram makes 1,187 allocations against Boost's 557,371. Per-site edge topology is built after the sweep from shared edges rather than per-site copies, and edges are sorted around each site by an overflow-safe pseudo-angle (0.10 changelog).
when_to_use: Games, procedural maps, stippling or Lloyd relaxation that need clipped Voronoi cells with ordered edge loops from thousands to a few hundred thousand points, in C or C++.

Replacing Boost.Polygon voronoi_diagram when the sites are points and you want edges already clipped to a box or convex polygon, without Boost headers (0.17 s vs 0.97 s clean build and a 33.7 KB vs 150.6 KB minimal executable in the author's table).
Allocation-sensitive or embedded code: jcv_diagram_generate_useralloc takes custom alloc/free callbacks, and generation does about a thousand allocations rather than hundreds of thousands.
Inputs with heavy symmetry or collinear structure, where 0.10's RAVL beachline keeps O(n log n) behaviour (100k pathological case 18.63 ms vs Boost 39.25 ms).
Browser or Node use via the npm jc-voronoi WebAssembly package when you need per-cell edge access.
when_not_to_use: Segment sites, medial axes or exact predicates: Boost.Polygon handles segment input with robust integer predicates; jc_voronoi is float-based Fortune on points and prunes duplicates and out-of-bounds points.
Raw Delaunay or Voronoi speed in JavaScript: the repo's own BENCHMARKS.md has d3-delaunay generating 100k random diagrams in 31.54 ms against JCV-wasm's 98.21 ms, with lower memory.
Upgrading from 0.9 just for speed on ordinary random input: at 100k random sites 0.9.0 (51.22 ms) is slightly faster than 0.10.0 (53.95 ms); 0.10 fixes worst-case scaling and memory instead.
Clipping to non-convex boundaries: only box and convex-polygon clippers ship (open issue #50 asks for non-convex).
Code that relied on the 0.9 API: 0.10 broke the edge API (jcv_graphedge, jcv_site.edges and jcv_diagram_get_next_edge removed) and changed struct layouts; see MIGRATION_GUIDE.md.

integration.form: header-only (stb-style: define JC_VORONOI_IMPLEMENTATION in one translation unit); optional jc_voronoi_clip.h; CMake target jc_voronoi::jc_voronoi, Homebrew tap, npm WebAssembly package
integration.min_toolchain: C99 (C11, C17 and C23 supported); includable from C++; the benchmark harness is C++11
integration.platforms: any; CI builds on macOS, Linux and Windows (MSVC build script provided); WebAssembly via Emscripten
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the header has no mutable global state (only static const values), and each call allocates its own context, so separate diagrams on separate threads look independent (inferred from source, not stated)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — covers point-site Voronoi (and Delaunay adjacency) with clipping included, but the API, coordinate type and output graph differ from Boost.Polygon's construct_voronoi/voronoi_diagram, and segment sites are not supported

gotchas: Sites come back sorted for the sweep, not in input order; use site->index to map back. The header comment on jcv_diagram_get_sites still says 'each index is the same as the original input point array', which contradicts the README and the 0.10 changelog.

Duplicate points, points outside the rect, and points rejected by the clipper are silently dropped, so diagram.numsites can be lower than num_points; with a NULL rect the bounds are computed automatically with 10 units of padding.

Default precision is float (JCV_REAL_TYPE); for large coordinate ranges or near-collinear input, switch to double by overriding JCV_REAL_TYPE, JCV_ATAN2, JCV_SQRT, JCV_FLT_MAX, JCV_REAL_TYPE_EPSILON and JCV_PI identically in every translation unit.

Allocation failures are not checked (the context block is memset straight after allocfn returns), and the fixed-size event-queue bound is guarded only by assert; several crash, infinite-loop and memory-blowup issues (#83, #85, #91) were closed during the July 2026 0.10 work.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Choose it over Delaunay32 or detria when you need Voronoi cells with clipped, ordered edge loops in plain C, not a triangulation; Delaunay32 (multithreaded, beats delaunator-cpp and Triangle) and detria (constrained Delaunay) are faster or stronger when the Delaunay triangulation itself is the output. Against CGAL-based Voronoi, it trades exact predicates for a dependency-free single header.
verified_claims_summary: The author's test/release-0.10.0-performance.md (Apple M5 Max, Apple clang 21.0.0, -O3 -DNDEBUG, medians with diagram destruction included) times jc_voronoi 0.10 against Boost.Polygon from Boost 1.92.0 at 178.00 us vs 649.83 us (1k random sites), 4.87 vs 6.82 ms (10k), 53.95 vs 80.21 ms (100k) and 18.63 vs 39.25 ms (100k pathological), with similar peak memory. The committed harness differs slightly from the published method: test/perftest.cpp seeds with srand(0) on a 4096-unit integer grid (the doc says seed 4), and compile_perftest.sh builds with -O2 -g, so reproducing the published numbers needs those settings changed.
status_note: Active (0.10.0 released 2026-07-22, last commit 2026-07-25, 733 stars, 129 commits on dev) and MIT-licensed, so copyable; the 0.10 rewrite is recent and broke the API, so pin a version.
